title: My Daily Routine
description: Wake up, pray, breakfast, work, the late lunch, the long Cairo evening — tell the shape of your ordinary day with the بـ present, and hear one verb change its face for I, you, he, she, we and they.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — first simplified video. A day-in-the-life vlog is watched with pictures only, then the same verbs are heard in the full بـ paradigm, then the learner narrates their own day in five sentences.
unlock_condition: Narrate your own day in ≥5 correct بـ-present sentences and score ≥12/16 on the who-is-doing-it listening sort
can_do: Describe your ordinary day with eight core verbs
Conjugate the Egyptian بـ present for every person
Ask what someone does every day

grammar.title: بـ in front, and the verb changes its face
grammar.explanation: Every Egyptian present-tense verb for a habit or something happening now starts with بـ. After it, the beginning of the verb tells you who: بروح is 'I go' (the بـ swallows the 'I' sound, so it is ba-, never ba-a-), بتروح is 'you' and also 'she', بيروح is 'he', بنروح is 'we'. Two endings finish the set: 'you (to a woman)' adds ـي (بتروحي) and 'you all' and 'they' add ـوا (بتروحوا، بيروحوا) — the alif at the end is written but never said. The same word covers 'I drink coffee' and 'I drink coffee every day', so you do not need a separate form for habits. Leave the بـ off only after words like عايز and لازم (عايز أشرب): a bare verb on its own is not a present tense in Egyptian.

examples.english: I go to work every day
Do you (f) drink coffee in the morning?

culture.title: A Cairo day starts late and ends later
culture.note: Ask when something happens and a Cairene often answers with a prayer, not a clock: بعد الفجر، بعد الضهر، بعد العصر، بعد المغرب، بعد العشا. The shape of the day follows: breakfast is often mid-morning, the real meal — الغدا — lands between three and five when people get home, and then comes a nap. Life restarts after sunset: shops stay open until midnight, visits begin at nine, and dinner (العشا) is at ten or later. If you arrange to meet someone بعد العصر you will sound local; if you turn up for dinner at seven you will find an empty table.

phrases.english: After the afternoon prayer, God willing

vocabulary.teaching_note: The first verb of every day-in-the-life vlog. Egyptians say بصحى; you will also hear بقوم ('I get up') for the same moment. The MSA أستيقظ is never said.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person sitting up in bed stretching, sunlight through a curtain, a phone alarm showing 7:00.

example.english: I wake up at seven every day

vocabulary.video_hint: The opening of a morning-routine vlog: alarm, bed, the vlogger saying بصحى / صحيت.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The verb the tea culture runs on. Notice بـ plus the 'I' form gives ba- in one syllable: bashrab, not ba-ashrab. That pattern holds for every verb in this lesson.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand lifting a small glass of red-brown tea to the mouth, steam rising.

example.english: I drink mint tea after lunch

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone pouring or sipping tea or coffee while narrating their morning.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The بـ meets a verb that starts with a hamza and the two melt into a long aa: باكل baakul. 'He eats' is بياكل biyaakul, 'we eat' بناكل — the same stretched vowel every time.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person eating fuul and bread from a small plate at a family table.

example.english: I eat with my family at night

vocabulary.video_hint: A family meal in a vlog; the vlogger saying باكل / بناكل as food is on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The most-used verb in the dialect. Egyptian 'go' is راح — the MSA أذهب marks you as reading from a textbook. The place follows directly with no 'to': بروح الشغل، بروح الجامعة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person walking out of an apartment-building door onto a busy Cairo street, bag over shoulder.

example.english: I go to work by metro

vocabulary.video_hint: Leaving the house or getting on the metro; بروح / بنروح said as the destination is named.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The verb for 'work' is اشتغل; the noun is الشغل. بتشتغل إيه؟ ('what do you do?') and بتشتغل فين؟ are the two questions every new acquaintance asks. Note the غ in the middle — a soft gargled g.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person at an office desk typing on a laptop, a lanyard round the neck, Cairo skyline through the window.

example.english: I work from nine to five

vocabulary.video_hint: Workplace or commute footage; the vlogger explaining what they do — بشتغل في…

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Egyptian word for studying your lessons is ذاكر — pronounced with a z, not th. Be careful: بدرس in Egypt usually means 'I teach', so a student says بذاكر.
vocabulary.image_scene: A student at a desk with open notebooks and a laptop, a university building through the window.
vocabulary.video_hint: Study-with-me vlogs; a student describing their day at university.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Long aa in the middle. The afternoon nap after الغدا is a real institution, so you will hear بنام شوية in the middle of the day, not only at night.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person asleep in bed, room dark, a fan turning on the ceiling.

example.english: I sleep very late at night

vocabulary.video_hint: The end of a day-in-the-life vlog; lights off, بنام or تصبحوا على خير.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The homecoming verb — 'I get back from work' is برجع من الشغل. Ends in ع, the deep throat sound; hold it rather than dropping it. The ج is a hard g: bargaʿ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person walking back in through an apartment door in the late afternoon, keys in hand.

example.english: I come back home at four

vocabulary.video_hint: Arriving home in a vlog; رجعت البيت or برجع as the door opens.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Five times a day, so it anchors every routine. The prayer name follows directly: بصلي الفجر، بصلي المغرب. Doubled ل — hold it. Christian Egyptians say the same verb for going to church prayers.
vocabulary.image_scene: A prayer mat laid out on a living-room floor, a person standing on it in prayer.

example.english: I pray Fajr and go back to sleep

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger mentioning prayer as a time marker — بعد ما أصلي — or a mosque visit.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Egyptian separates 'watch' from 'see': you watch TV with اتفرج على, you see a friend with شاف. The على is part of the verb — بتفرج على التليفزيون، بتفرج على ماتش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family on a sofa watching a large TV in the evening, tea glasses on the coffee table.

example.english: At night I watch a series

vocabulary.video_hint: Evening scenes with a TV or phone on; بتفرج / بنتفرج said about a show or match.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Put it at the start or the end of the sentence — both are natural. It is the phrase that turns a verb into a habit. يوم has the Egyptian oo vowel, not the MSA yawm.
vocabulary.image_scene: A wall calendar with every day of the week ticked in green.

example.english: Every day I drink tea in the morning

vocabulary.video_hint: Routine narration — كل يوم بصحى… — at the start of a day vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Written عادة or عادةً online; said ʿaadatan. Its close cousin غالباً means 'mostly'. Careful: عادي — the same letters minus the ending — means 'normal / no big deal', a very different word you will hear constantly.
vocabulary.image_scene: A weekly planner with the same coffee-cup icon drawn in most, but not all, of the mornings.

example.english: Usually I have lunch at four

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger explaining a habit — عادةً بروح… — with the activity on screen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Breakfast is الفطار and the verb is فطر. فطرت؟ ('have you had breakfast?') works as a mid-morning greeting. In Ramadan the same verb means breaking the fast at sunset.
vocabulary.image_scene: A breakfast spread of fuul, ta'miyya, bread, white cheese and a glass of tea on a small table.

example.english: I have fuul and ta'miyya for breakfast

vocabulary.video_hint: Breakfast in a morning vlog; the word فطار as the food is shown.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Lunch is الغدا, the main meal of the day, and it has its own verb. اتغديت؟ ('have you had lunch?') is a real question at four in the afternoon. Doubled د — hold it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A large pot of molokhia, rice and chicken in the middle of a family table in the late afternoon.

example.english: I have lunch at home with Mum

vocabulary.video_hint: The late-afternoon family meal; الغدا named, or the question اتغديت؟

vocabulary.teaching_note: Dinner is العشا and comes late — ten at night is normal, and it is lighter than lunch. The verb pairs with بتغدى; learn them together. Doubled ش.
vocabulary.image_scene: A late-night table with bread, cheese, eggs and a plate of fruit, a clock on the wall showing 10:00.

example.english: I have dinner late, at ten

vocabulary.video_hint: Evening home dinner or a late restaurant scene; العشا said as the food arrives.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A true Egyptian marker — MSA has مبكراً, which nobody says. Its opposite, متأخر, you will meet in the examples; both go at the end of the sentence: بصحى بدري، بنام متأخر.
vocabulary.image_scene: An alarm clock showing 5:30 next to a window with the first grey light of dawn.

example.english: I wake up early because of work

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger complaining or boasting about the hour — صحيت بدري النهارده.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The step after waking: بصحى is opening your eyes, بقوم is leaving the bed. The ق is a glottal stop here — baʾuum — the everyday Cairo sound of the letter.
vocabulary.image_scene: A person swinging their legs out of bed and standing up, slippers on the floor.

example.arabic: بقوم من السرير الساعة سبعة ونص
example.transliteration: baʾuum min es-siriir es-saaʿa sabʿa wi-nuṣṣ
example.english: I get out of bed at half past seven

vocabulary.video_hint: Getting out of bed in a morning-routine vlog; قمت / بقوم as the feet hit the floor.

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.arabic: بتعمل إيه كل يوم يا كريم؟
dialogue.transliteration: bitiʿmil eeh kull yoom ya kariim?
dialogue.english: What do you do every day, Karim?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: I wake up at six and pray Fajr

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: I have breakfast and go to work at eight

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.english: When do you get back home?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: برجع الساعة أربعة، بتغدى وبنام شوية
dialogue.transliteration: bargaʿ es-saaʿa arbaʿa, batghadda wi-banaam shwayya
dialogue.english: I get back at four, have lunch and sleep a bit

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: عادةً بتفرج على مسلسل مع عيلتي
dialogue.transliteration: ʿaadatan batfarrag ʿala musalsal maʿa ʿeelti
dialogue.english: Usually I watch a series with my family

sound_spotlight.explanation: The 'I' prefix أ disappears inside the بـ: you say bashrab in two beats, never ba-ashrab. In captions you will see بشرب, sometimes بأشرب — hear them both as ba-.
'He' keeps its يـ after the بـ, so it sounds like biy-: biyruuḥ. In fast speech the i is tiny — listen for the y that tells 'he' apart from 'you' (bitruuḥ).
'They' and 'you all' end in ـوا, written with an alif that is never pronounced. The vowel is a plain u: biyruuḥu. Do not read it as -uwa.

lesson_sequence.detail: A 60-second Cairo day-in-the-life clip plays with no text — alarm, prayer mat, fuul breakfast, the metro. One English line: today you learn to tell your day.
Seventeen cards, each with its illustration and native audio in the 'I' form. Tap to hear the 'he' and 'you' forms underneath.
The paradigm table for بروح builds row by row with audio; then the learner drags pronouns onto blank verb forms for بشرب and بشتغل.
Listening sort: sixteen short clips (بروح، بتروحي، بيناموا…) sorted into I / you / he / she / we / they buckets. Immediate feedback with the prefix and ending highlighted.
The same 60-second clip now with Egyptian captions; the learner taps every بـ verb they recognise. Recognised verbs light up in the paradigm table.
Five prompts (wake up, breakfast, go to, come back, night) — the learner records one sentence each. Fluency feedback, no grading beyond verb form.
Words-learned counter rolls up. Nudge: tomorrow, narrate your morning in your head in Egyptian as you do it.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tomorrow morning, say each step out loud as you do it: بصحى… بشرب شاي… بفطر… بروح الشغل.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-morning notification. Activates the routine verbs in the here-and-now while the actions are happening.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask an Egyptian friend or tutor: بتعمل إيه كل يوم؟ — and listen for the prayer times and meals they use as clock markers.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen; a tutor-ready question that elicits the whole paradigm in the answers.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Find an Egyptian day-in-the-life vlog and count how many times you hear بروح / بنروح. Write the number down.
real_world_prompts.context: Optional homework card. Passive recognition of the highest-frequency verb in authentic speech.

video_needs.scene: A vlogger narrating their day in the بـ present while the actions are on screen: waking up, praying, fuul for breakfast, the metro to work, the late lunch, a series at night.
